titulo: Closer to home: how nearshoring and friend-shoring are redrawing the map of global production

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: On the outskirts of an industrial city in northern Mexico, land that once grew sorghum is disappearing under concrete. Rows of identical warehouses, painted white and grey, stretch towards the horizon, and the lorries queuing at their gates carry the logos of companies from Asia, North America and Europe. Local officials talk proudly of a boom. Economists prefer a more technical term for what is happening here and in a growing number of places around the world: nearshoring.

The idea is simple. After decades in which manufacturers chased the lowest possible costs, often thousands of kilometres away from their customers, many are now moving production closer to the markets they serve. A related concept, friend-shoring, goes a step further: it means sourcing from countries considered politically reliable, even if they are not geographically close. Both reflect the same underlying shift, from a model obsessed with efficiency to one that places a premium on resilience, and both are reshaping investment decisions on every continent.

The trigger was a succession of shocks. The pandemic closed factories and ports and exposed how dependent Western economies had become on a handful of suppliers for everything from face masks to microchips. Freight rates for a standard container on the main Asia–Europe routes multiplied several times over in a matter of months. Then came the war in Ukraine, which turned energy into a weapon, and mounting tension between the United States and China, which raised the prospect of sanctions, export controls and tariffs on a wide range of goods.

‘For years, the question we asked was how cheap a supplier could be,’ says the operations director of a European car-parts company that has opened a second plant in Mexico to serve its North American clients. ‘Now the first question is whether the goods will actually arrive.’ Her company still produces in Asia, but it has adopted what managers call a ‘China plus one’ strategy: keep existing facilities, but add capacity elsewhere so that no single country can bring the whole operation to a halt.

Mexico is one of the clearest beneficiaries. Its long border with the United States, its free-trade agreement with its two northern neighbours and its relatively low labour costs have made it a natural destination. In recent years it has overtaken China as the largest source of American imports, a milestone loaded with symbolism. Similar stories can be told about Vietnam and India, and about the periphery of Europe, where Poland, Romania or Morocco, just across the Strait of Gibraltar, are attracting investment from firms that want to serve the European market from closer to home.

Governments have actively encouraged the trend. Washington has offered generous tax credits for clean-energy and semiconductor production on American soil, while the European Union has adopted legislation aiming to raise its share of global chip manufacturing and to secure supplies of critical raw materials such as lithium and rare earths. Industrial policy, long regarded with suspicion in liberal economies, is back in fashion, and subsidies have become a tool of geopolitical competition. Critics warn of a costly subsidy race in which wealthy countries outbid each other while poorer ones cannot compete.

Yet the data tell a more nuanced story than the headlines. When researchers trace supply chains in detail, they often find that goods once imported directly from China now arrive via Mexico or Vietnam, but contain a significant share of Chinese components. In other words, the chains have been lengthened and rerouted rather than truly shortened. Chinese companies themselves are among the most active investors in Mexican industrial parks, keen to keep access to the American market. Dependence has, in many cases, simply moved one link further back.

Moreover, relocation is costly. Building a factory takes years, training a workforce takes longer, and the dense networks of suppliers that make certain Asian regions so efficient cannot be replicated overnight. In northern Mexico, the boom has strained water supplies, electricity grids and roads; local businesses complain of shortages of skilled technicians and of rising wages. Several surveys of executives suggest that, while many companies talk enthusiastically about nearshoring, a much smaller number have actually moved a significant part of their production.

Friend-shoring raises questions of its own. Who counts as a friend, and for how long? Alliances shift, and a country deemed reliable today may adopt a very different stance after its next election. Developing economies, in particular, fear being forced to choose sides in a contest between blocs, losing access to markets or investment as a result. International institutions have warned that a fragmentation of the world economy into rival blocs could reduce global output by several percentage points in the long run, with poorer countries bearing a disproportionate share of the cost.

There is also the matter of prices. Global supply chains delivered cheap goods for decades, contributing to the low inflation that prevailed in rich countries until recently. Reorganising them for security rather than efficiency is likely to raise production costs, at least in the short term. Consumers may end up paying a ‘resilience premium’, and central banks may discover that the disinflationary tailwind of globalisation has turned into a mild headwind.

For Spain and other southern European countries, the reshuffle presents a genuine opportunity. Abundant renewable energy, available industrial land, a skilled workforce and proximity to North Africa could make the Iberian Peninsula an attractive base for firms seeking to bring production back to Europe. Investments in battery plants and green hydrogen have already been announced, although turning announcements into functioning factories remains a challenge, and competition from Central Europe and Morocco is fierce. Permitting delays and grid connections, rather than wages, are often cited by investors as the main obstacles.

Back in northern Mexico, the lorries keep queuing. The new map of global production is still being drawn, and it is unlikely to resemble either the hyper-globalised world of the early 2000s or the self-sufficient blocs that some politicians promise. More plausibly, it will be a patchwork: shorter chains for strategic goods, global ones for almost everything else, and a constant balancing act between the cost of efficiency and the price of security.
titulo_es: Más cerca de casa: cómo la relocalización cercana y entre aliados está redibujando el mapa de la producción mundial
resumen_es: Reportaje sobre el traslado de la producción a países cercanos o aliados (nearshoring y friend-shoring) tras la pandemia y las tensiones geopolíticas, con México como ejemplo y sus límites, costes y oportunidades para España.

ideas_clave.idea: Companies are relocating production closer to their markets or to politically allied countries, prioritising resilience over pure cost efficiency.
The pandemic, soaring freight costs, the war in Ukraine and US–China rivalry pushed firms to diversify, for example through a ‘China plus one’ approach.
Mexico, thanks to its location, trade agreement and wages, is a major winner, alongside Vietnam, India and countries on Europe’s periphery.
Governments in the US and the EU are fostering the shift through subsidies and industrial policy, raising fears of a subsidy race.
In practice, supply chains have often been rerouted rather than shortened, as Chinese inputs and investors remain present in the new hubs.
Relocation is slow and expensive, strains local infrastructure and has been less widespread than the rhetoric suggests.
Friend-shoring is complicated by shifting alliances and could fragment the world economy, hurting poorer countries most.
Prioritising security over efficiency is likely to raise costs and add inflationary pressure.
Spain could benefit thanks to renewables, land and workers, although obstacles and competition remain.
The future is likely to be a mixed model, combining short chains for strategic goods with global ones for the rest.

resumen_modelo: The report examines how firms are reorganising global supply chains by moving production closer to their customers (nearshoring) or to politically reliable countries (friend-shoring), thereby giving priority to resilience over cost. This shift was triggered by a series of shocks: the pandemic, which revealed excessive dependence on a few suppliers, the surge in freight costs, the war in Ukraine and growing tension between the United States and China. Many companies have therefore opted to keep their Asian plants while adding capacity elsewhere. Mexico stands out as a major beneficiary, along with Vietnam, India and parts of Europe’s periphery, and governments are reinforcing the trend with subsidies and industrial policy. Nevertheless, the author points out that the reality is more complex than the headlines suggest. Supply chains have frequently been rerouted rather than shortened, as Chinese components and investors remain involved; relocation is slow and costly and strains local infrastructure; and friend-shoring depends on shifting alliances, with a risk of fragmentation that would hurt developing countries in particular. In addition, putting security before efficiency is likely to push up prices. Spain is presented as a potential winner, given its renewable energy and industrial land, provided it overcomes administrative hurdles. The article concludes that the emerging model will probably be a hybrid, balancing efficiency against security.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The land where the new warehouses are being built was previously used to grow maize.
preguntas.cita: land that once grew sorghum is disappearing under concrete
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que en esos terrenos se cultivaba sorgo, no maíz. Se ha cambiado un detalle.

preguntas.pregunta: How does friend-shoring differ from nearshoring?
opciones: It means producing only in one’s own country
It means sourcing from politically reliable countries, even if they are far away
It means choosing the cheapest supplier regardless of location
It means sharing factories with competitors
respuestas: It means sourcing from politically reliable countries, even if they are far away
preguntas.cita: it means sourcing from countries considered politically reliable, even if they are not geographically close
preguntas.explicacion: El friend-shoring prima la fiabilidad política del país proveedor, no la cercanía geográfica. Producir en el propio país sería reshoring, y buscar el proveedor más barato es el modelo anterior.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 2 una expresión que signifique «controles a la exportación».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘government restrictions on selling certain goods abroad’.
preguntas.cita: which raised the prospect of sanctions, export controls and tariffs
preguntas.explicacion: «Export controls» son restricciones a la exportación de determinados bienes o tecnologías, como los semiconductores avanzados.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Container freight rates between Asia and Europe multiplied during the pandemic.
preguntas.cita: Freight rates for a standard container on the main Asia–Europe routes multiplied several times over in a matter of months.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que los fletes se multiplicaron varias veces en pocos meses, en el contexto de la pandemia.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the ‘China plus one’ strategy described by the operations director?
respuestas: It consists of keeping existing factories in China or Asia while adding production capacity in another country, so that a problem in a single country cannot stop the whole business.
preguntas.cita: keep existing facilities, but add capacity elsewhere so that no single country can bring the whole operation to a halt
preguntas.explicacion: No se trata de abandonar China, sino de diversificar para reducir el riesgo de depender de un solo país.

preguntas.pregunta: Which of these factors is NOT mentioned as an advantage of Mexico?
opciones: Its border with the United States
Its free-trade agreement with its northern neighbours
preguntas.cita: Its long border with the United States, its free-trade agreement with its two northern neighbours and its relatively low labour costs
preguntas.explicacion: Las tres primeras ventajas aparecen en el párrafo 4. El agua no es una ventaja: en el párrafo 7 se dice que el auge ha tensionado el suministro de agua.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The European Union has set a target of producing half of the world’s microchips.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que la UE quiere aumentar su cuota en la fabricación mundial de chips, pero no da ninguna cifra objetivo.

preguntas.pregunta: What do detailed studies of supply chains often reveal?
opciones: That chains have become much shorter
That goods from Mexico or Vietnam still contain many Chinese components
That Chinese companies have left Mexico
That dependence on Asia has disappeared
respuestas: That goods from Mexico or Vietnam still contain many Chinese components
preguntas.cita: goods once imported directly from China now arrive via Mexico or Vietnam, but contain a significant share of Chinese components
preguntas.explicacion: Los estudios muestran que las cadenas se han desviado y alargado, no acortado, y que la dependencia se ha desplazado un eslabón atrás. Las empresas chinas, de hecho, invierten en México.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 7 una palabra que signifique «sometido a presión, sobrecargado».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘put under excessive pressure’.
preguntas.cita: the boom has strained water supplies, electricity grids and roads
preguntas.explicacion: «To strain» significa forzar o sobrecargar; aquí, el auge industrial ha llevado al límite el agua, la red eléctrica y las carreteras.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: According to international institutions, fragmentation into blocs would mainly hurt rich countries.
preguntas.cita: with poorer countries bearing a disproportionate share of the cost
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que los países más pobres soportarían una parte desproporcionada del coste, no los ricos.

preguntas.pregunta: Why might nearshoring and friend-shoring have consequences for inflation?
respuestas: Because global supply chains helped keep goods cheap and inflation low for decades. Reorganising them for security rather than efficiency raises production costs, so consumers may pay a ‘resilience premium’ and globalisation would stop pushing inflation down.
preguntas.cita: Reorganising them for security rather than efficiency is likely to raise production costs, at least in the short term.
preguntas.explicacion: La respuesta debe relacionar el fin de la eficiencia máxima con costes más altos y explicar el paso de «viento de cola» desinflacionista a «viento de cara».

preguntas.pregunta: According to investors, what are often the main obstacles to investing in Spain?
preguntas.cita: Permitting delays and grid connections, rather than wages, are often cited by investors as the main obstacles.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto señala los retrasos en los permisos y las conexiones a la red, no los salarios. La energía renovable y el suelo industrial se presentan como ventajas.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 11 una palabra que signifique «mosaico, conjunto heterogéneo».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘a mixture of different elements’.
preguntas.explicacion: «Patchwork» es literalmente una labor de retales; en sentido figurado, un conjunto heterogéneo de elementos distintos.

ideas: Nearshoring: closer to the final market
Reshoring: back to the home country

tribunal.pregunta: What is the EU doing to reduce its strategic dependencies?
tribunal.pista_es: Política industrial europea: chips, materias primas críticas, autonomía estratégica abierta.

tribunal.pregunta: Could Spain become a winner of nearshoring? What should it do to attract investment?
tribunal.pista_es: Relación con España: ventajas, obstáculos y políticas (permisos, red eléctrica, fondos europeos).
ideas: Cheap renewable energy and available land
Speed up permits and grid connections
Use of EU recovery funds and strategic projects

ideas: Risk of protectionism disguised as security
